contexts.park_guell:
Park Güell (part of Park Güell). Materials: local stone (viaducts and columns), trencadís (broken tile/ceramic mosaic). Inspired by the English garden-city movement (hence the English word 'Park' in its name); marks Gaudí's 'naturalist period', in which his study of nature and organic forms drove both ornament and underlying structural geometry. Symbolic references throughout include political Catalanism (entrance stairway) and Catholicism (the Calvary, originally conceived as a chapel). Uses inverted catenary arches for its viaducts and elevated pathways, the same load-bearing-compression method Gaudí used earlier at Colònia Güell. Entry to the Monumental Zone (main terrace, mosaics, viaducts, gate area) has required a paid ticket since October 2013; Barcelona residents enter free. UNESCO's 1984 inscription describes the park's architecture as combining the Arts and Crafts movement, Symbolism, Expressionism, and Rationalism, and as having presaged techniques of 20th-century Modernism. Introduced curved, undulating benches at Park Güell -- a precursor to the style Gaudí later fully realized at the Sagrada Família.
---

Related: Catenary/compression structural logic shared with catenaria_pedrera, though executed in stone viaducts here versus brick vaulting there.
contexts.drac_park_guell:
El Drac (Dragon / Salamander) (part of park_guell). Materials: trencadís (tile-shard mosaic), masonry/mortar core. Popularly associated with mythological guardian-dragon imagery, though sources disagree on whether the figure represents a dragon or a salamander -- the official park site itself uses both terms. Functions as the overflow spout of the park's rainwater system: water falling on the Greek Theatre/Nature Square above is collected by a conduit inside the Hypostyle Room's colonnade and channeled to an underground cistern, with the dragon's mouth as that system's overflow outlet. Covered in trencadís (tile-shard mosaic); the official park site calls it 'the most popular image of the park.' Sits on the Dragon Stairway, a twin flight of steps divided into three landings: goblin-like shapes on the first landing, the emblem of Catalonia on the second, and the dragon/salamander further up.

contexts.porxada_bugaderia:
Pòrtic de la Bugaderia (Laundry Room Portico / Washerwoman's Portico) (part of park_guell). Materials: unworked (rough-cut) hillside stone. Described by the park's own site as taking 'the shape of a great wave atop slanting columns' -- called one of the finest examples of Gaudí's organic architecture; the slanted double colonnade evokes a stone forest, echoing how the park's viaduct columns and vaults elsewhere mimic tree trunks and natural forms. The double colonnade of slanting columns acts as a structural buttress against the retaining wall behind it -- the tilt is load-bearing, not decorative. Uses the same structural logic as the park's viaducts: inclined stone columns form a parabola/inverted-catenary profile so the columns work in pure compression along the line of thrust, without needing external buttressing.

contexts.porters_lodge_park_guell:
Porter's Lodge (entrance gatehouses) (part of park_guell). Materials: . Whimsical, fairy-tale-like pavilion forms marking the park's main entrance, reflecting Güell's ambition to recreate an English residential-park model. One of the two pavilions originally housed a phone booth; the other now contains a permanent exhibit of the Barcelona City History Museum. Forms a pair of gatehouses flanking the park's main entrance, among the first structures built on site.

contexts.banc_serpentejant:
Serpentine Bench (Banc de trencadís) (part of park_guell). Materials: trencadís (broken tile/ceramic/glass mosaic). Its ergonomic, curving form creates enclaves along its length that encourage social interaction rather than facing visitors outward in a straight line. Sits directly atop the Hypostyle Room's vaulted terrace, following the ergonomic curve designed to double as a shared social space rather than a simple boundary wall. One of Gaudí's introductions of curved, undulating bench forms at Park Güell, a precursor to the style he later fully realized at the Sagrada Família.

Functions as part of the park's rainwater collection system: a conduit inside the colonnade gathers water falling on the terrace above and channels it to an underground cistern, ultimately overflowing through the dragon's mouth (see drac_park_guell). Ceiling mosaics recall grotesque motifs inspired by Roman architecture, particularly the Domus Aurea.

contexts.viaductes_park_guell:
Viaducts / elevated pathways (part of park_guell). Materials: local stone. Columns and vaulted supports mimic tree trunks and natural forms, blending the paths seamlessly with the surrounding landscape. As with Gaudí's earlier work at Colònia Güell, the viaducts use inverted catenary arches to achieve optimal load-bearing compression, so the stone columns work in pure compression without needing external buttressing. Columns and vaulted supports mimic tree trunks and natural forms, part of Gaudí's naturalist-period design language for the park.

contexts.la_pedrera:
Casa Milà (La Pedrera) (part of Casa Milà (La Pedrera)). Materials: limestone (Garraf Massif, lower floor; Villefranche quarry, upper floors), wrought iron, curved iron floor beams. Gaudí designed the house as 'a constant curve, both outside and inside,' combining ruled geometry with naturalistic form. There is no agreement on which mountain inspired the facade -- candidates proposed by different contemporaries include the rocks of Fray Guerau in the Prades mountains, St. Miquel del Fai, the Torrent de Pareis cliffs in Menorca, Uçhisar in Cappadocia, and Mola Gallifa. Self-supporting stone facade with no load-bearing walls, connected to curved iron beams surrounding the perimeter of each floor -- allowing interior walls to be added or removed without affecting the building's stability. In August 1908 the City Council fined the project for exceeding its permitted height and site boundaries; the dispute was resolved in December 1909 when the building was certified as monumental and exempted from strict bylaw compliance. Nicknamed 'La Pedrera' ('the stone quarry') by residents who disliked its rough-hewn, undulating stone facade -- an insult that became its popular name. Considered a predecessor of later biomorphic buildings such as the 1921 Einstein Tower (Erich Mendelsohn), the Guggenheim Museum (Frank Wright), and Frank Gehry's Disney Concert Hall.
---

contexts.catenaria_pedrera:
Espai Gaudí attic (catenary/parabolic brick arches) (part of la_pedrera). Materials: brick (volta catalana / timbrel vaulting). The rippling roofline is widely compared to the ribs of a huge animal or the fronds of a palm; the space, now called Espai Gaudí, is often described as feeling like walking through the inside of a whale's ribcage. Built using volta catalana (Catalan/timbrel vault) technique -- thin layered brick vaulting imported from Italy in the 14th century, laid without a full wooden centering framework. Arch height and spacing directly follow the courtyards' footprint below: arches rise higher where the plan narrows and drop lower where it widens, so the roof structure encloses the irregular figure-8 courtyard shape beneath it. 270 parabolic brick arches of varying height, spaced about 80 cm apart, give the roofline a rippling, organic silhouette.

contexts.caps_pedrera:
Chimneys and rooftop sculptures ('caps') (part of la_pedrera). Materials: brick, lime coating, broken marble, broken Valencia tiles, glass (one chimney). Nicknamed the 'garden of warriors' by poet Pere Gimferrer, since the grouped chimneys look like helmeted sentinels standing guard over the skylight/staircase exits; their helmet-like silhouettes are sometimes linked to Gaudí's interest in medieval fortress architecture. The roof holds 28 chimneys in several groupings, 6 skylight/staircase exits, 2 half-hidden vents that renew air inside the building, and 4 discharge domes -- all functional rather than purely decorative. Some staircase-exit towers double as housings for the building's water tanks, a few of which are snail-shaped. The rooftop underwent a later restoration that removed chimneys added after Gaudí's death, TV antennas, and other additions, to return the roofscape closer to its originally designed functional layout. One chimney is topped with glass -- reportedly added by Gaudí the day after the building's inauguration party using empty champagne bottles, later restored with early-20th-century champagne-bottle bases.
---

contexts.facana_pedrera:
Self-supporting stone facade (part of la_pedrera). Materials: limestone (Garraf Massif, first floor), limestone (Villefranche quarry, higher levels), wrought iron (balconies). Viewed from outside, the building reads in three parts: the main six-storey block with winding stone floors, two set-back floors with a smoother, whiter, wave-like curve, and the body of the roof. Self-supporting: free of load-bearing walls, with the facade connected to curved iron beams around the perimeter of each floor, allowing large window openings and free interior layouts. Original lower-level wrought ironwork was removed in 1928 when a tailor's shop opened in the building; one surviving balcony grille was later donated to MoMA, where it is on display. The undulating, rough-hewn stone facade and twisting wrought-iron balconies were controversial when built, giving rise to the 'La Pedrera' (stone quarry) nickname.
---

contexts.patis_pedrera:
Courtyards and interior gate (part of la_pedrera). Materials: cast iron (pillars, beams), wrought iron (gate). The floor-support beam structure was interpreted by Josep Maria Carandell, who built the centerpiece at a shipyard, as representing the helm of a ship -- 'the soul of the building,' with a resemblance to Gothic crypts. The iron entrance gate's non-symmetrical structure evokes soap bubbles formed between the hands, or the structure of a plant cell. The courtyard floor's central support girder combines two concentric cylindrical beams with stretched radial beams, functioning as a keystone working in both tension and compression -- structurally described as 'the soul of the building.' The interior iron gate originally served both pedestrians and cars, providing access to the basement garage (now an auditorium). The two entrance halls are fully polychrome, with oil paintings on the plaster surfaces referencing mythology and flowers.

contexts.sagrada_familia:
Sagrada Família (part of Sagrada Família). Materials: piedra de Montjuïc (fases iniciales), piedra de la cantera de Withnell, Inglaterra (desde 2018), piedra postensada (fases finales de construcción), mosaico de vidrio veneciano (pináculos). Concebida como 'templo expiatorio' financiado solo con donaciones privadas, inspirado en la basílica de Loreto tras un viaje de Bocabella al Vaticano en 1872; combina formas góticas con el Art Nouveau curvilíneo propio de Gaudí. Las columnas interiores son un diseño único de Gaudí: su sección pasa de cuadrada a octogonal, luego a dieciséis lados y finalmente a circular, por intersección de columnas helicoidales. La fachada de la Pasión contiene un cuadrado mágico basado en el de la Melencolia I (1514) de Durero, donde filas y columnas suman 33. La torre de Jesucristo se diseñó deliberadamente 1 metro más baja que la montaña de Montjuïc, porque Gaudí creía que su obra no debía superar la de Dios. El templo tiene tres grandes fachadas: Natividad (la más ornamentada, terminada antes de 1936), Pasión (austera, de líneas duras, obra escultórica de Josep Maria Subirachs) y Gloria (la más grande, aún incompleta). Los chapiteles representan, de menor a mayor altura, a los Doce Apóstoles, los cuatro Evangelistas, la Virgen María y, el más alto, Jesucristo.
---
Related: Mismo arquitecto (Antoni Gaudí) que park_guell, la_pedrera y casa_batllo; forma parte, solo parcialmente (cripta y fachada de la Natividad), de la inscripción UNESCO 'Obras de Antoni Gaudí' de 2005 -- a diferencia de park_guell y la_pedrera, que fueron incluidos enteros en 1984.
contexts.cupula_sagrada_familia:
Bóvedas hiperboloides del crucero y torre de Jesucristo (part of sagrada_familia). Materials: piedra postensada. Gaudí quiso que, desde la entrada principal, el visitante pudiera ver en perspectiva ascendente las bóvedas de la nave, el crucero y el ábside. El uso de formas hiperboloides se acentúa en el diseño posterior de Gaudí, sobre todo a partir de 1914. La torre de Jesucristo, con sus 172.5 m, convirtió a la Sagrada Família en la iglesia más alta del mundo, superando en 11 m al anterior récord, la catedral de Ulm.

contexts.facana_naixement:
Fachada de la Natividad (part of sagrada_familia). Materials: piedra tallada a mano. Dedicada al nacimiento de Jesús; orientada al noreste, hacia el sol naciente, como símbolo del nacimiento de Cristo. Gaudí la eligió como la primera en construirse por ser, en su opinión, la más atractiva y accesible al público. En la base de cada uno de los grandes pilares que separan los pórticos hay una tortuga (una terrestre, otra marina), símbolo del tiempo inmutable; dos camaleones a los lados simbolizan el cambio. El Árbol de la Vida se alza sobre la puerta de Jesús, en el pórtico de la Caridad. Gaudí quería que toda la fachada estuviera policromada, con cada arquivolta y figura pintada, para que los personajes parecieran tan vivos como las plantas y animales representados.

Dedicada a la Pasión y muerte de Cristo, orientada al oeste (sol poniente, símbolo de la muerte de Cristo); Gaudí quería que provocara miedo en quien la contemplara, con arcos 'rotos' y columnas 'cortadas' y fuertes claroscuros. Contiene un cuadrado mágico basado en el de la Melencolia I de Durero (1514), modificado para que filas y columnas sumen 33 en vez de 34. Las escenas se organizan en tres niveles ascendentes en forma de S que reproducen el Vía Crucis: la Última Cena y el beso de Judas abajo, el Calvario en el nivel medio, y la Muerte, Sepultura y Resurrección arriba. Cada uno de los cuatro chapiteles está dedicado a un apóstol (Santiago, Tomás, Felipe y Bartolomé).

contexts.torres_sagrada_familia:
Chapiteles y torres (part of sagrada_familia). Materials: piedra, mosaico de vidrio veneciano (remates). Dieciocho chapiteles previstos, en orden ascendente de altura: los Doce Apóstoles, los cuatro Evangelistas, la Virgen María y, el más alto, Jesucristo. Los remates de los chapiteles más bajos representan hostias con espigas de trigo y cálices con racimos de uva, símbolos eucarísticos. El 29 de noviembre de 2021 se instaló una estrella de cristal iluminada de doce puntas y 7 m en la torre dedicada a la Virgen María. Los remates geométricos de los chapiteles de la fachada de la Natividad recuerdan al cubismo, aunque el estilo de Gaudí se inspiraba en la naturaleza, no en otros movimientos artísticos.

contexts.casa_batllo:
Casa Batlló (part of Casa Batlló). Materials: piedra arenisca de Montjuïc, trencadís (mosaico de cerámica), discos de vidrio de colores, cerámica policromada (330 piezas), hierro forjado. Encargada en plena rivalidad de las familias burguesas de Passeig de Gràcia (la 'Illa de la Discòrdia'): el industrial textil Josep Batlló quiso una casa que 'pusiera en su lugar' a los edificios vecinos de Puig i Cadafalch y Domènech i Montaner. El desván tiene sesenta arcos catenarios que crean un espacio que evoca la caja torácica de un animal. El patio de luces central está revestido de azulejos en tonalidades de azul graduadas (más intensas arriba, más claras abajo) para repartir la luz de forma uniforme entre pisos. El nombre popular 'Casa dels Ossos' (Casa de los Huesos) responde a su estética biomórfica y esquelética. La cubierta, de perfil arqueado, evoca el lomo de un dragón o dinosaurio; una interpretación habitual sitúa la torre con cruz como la lanza de Sant Jordi clavada en el lomo de la bestia.

contexts.pla_frontal_casa_batllo:
Fachada principal (planta frontal) (part of casa_batllo). Materials: piedra arenisca de Montjuïc (planta baja y galerías del primer piso), discos de vidrio de colores, 330 piezas de cerámica policromada, hierro forjado (balcones). La sección central evoca la superficie de un lago con nenúfares, con reminiscencias de los Nenúfares de Monet, mediante el efecto ondulante del mosaico de vidrio y cerámica. El remate superior muestra un friso de piezas cerámicas de interpretación diversa; Gaudí reutilizó fragmentos de trencadís procedentes de descartes de otras obras. Las tejas del tejado, con acabado metálico, simulan las escamas de un monstruo, degradándose del verde (donde empieza la cabeza) al azul y violeta en el centro, y al rojo y rosa en el extremo izquierdo. La torre rematada en cruz de cuatro brazos orientados a los puntos cardinales lleva monogramas de Jesús (JHS), María (M con corona ducal) y José (JHP) en piezas de cerámica dorada. Un pequeño ventanal triangular en el tejado simula el ojo del dragón.

La planta baja es la parte más llamativa del edificio, con tracería inusual, ventanas ovaladas irregulares y piedra tallada con formas sinuosas, casi sin líneas rectas. Las formas redondeadas de los huecos y los bordes labrados a modo de labios dan a la planta baja el sobrenombre de 'casa dels badalls' (casa de los bostezos). Seis finas columnas frente a los grandes ventanales simulan los huesos de una extremidad con una articulación central, aunque en realidad son decoración floral.
